harbor.practice: Harbor release r2026.11.3 maps code SHA, prompt versions, tool schemas, model revision, embedder + index, ACL watermark and eval suite.
harbor.failure: Rolling back code only, while an incompatible prompt, index or adapter stays live.
harbor.fitNote: one release ID for code, prompts, model and index
harbor.tryIt: Write Harbor's release manifest for r2026.11.3 as a file, then change only the prompt version and write the new release ID. Check that traces would show which release served each answer.

store.practice: {company} changes prompts and the product index more often than code. Each change creates a new release manifest, so a bad answer during a sale can be traced to the exact prompt, model and index that produced it.
store.failure: Rolling back code after a bad sale-day answer, while the new prompt and index stay live.
store.tryIt: Write {company}'s release manifest with code SHA, prompt versions, tool schemas, model, embedder, index version and evaluation suite. Then list which fields change most often.

bank.practice: {company} must be able to show which system produced any letter or summary. Every trace carries the release ID, and every release manifest is kept for the full audit retention period.
bank.failure: Keeping only the code history, so nobody can say which prompt drafted a disputed letter.
bank.tryIt: Write the audit question “which system drafted this letter?” as a lookup: trace → release ID → manifest fields. List what must be kept, and for how long.

travel.practice: {company}'s manifest includes the version of each supplier tool schema, because a supplier API change can break rebooking without any code change on {company}'s side.
travel.failure: Leaving tool schemas out of the manifest, so a schema change is invisible in release history.
travel.tryIt: Write {company}'s manifest and add a field for each supplier tool schema version. Then describe a regression you could bisect with it.

harbor.practice: The same signed Harbor image and model artifact tested in staging is promoted to production; only credentials and capacity differ.
harbor.failure: A container that downloads "latest" model weights at start-up; the release is not reproducible.
harbor.fitNote: the same signed image in staging and production
harbor.tryIt: Step through the promotion figure and write, for each stage, which artefact digests stay the same and which configuration values differ.

store.practice: {company}'s GPU pools, vector database, queues and alerts are defined in code and applied by a pipeline. Pre-sale scaling is a reviewed change, not a console click.
store.failure: Scaling GPU pools by hand before a sale, then losing the settings when the cluster is rebuilt.
store.tryIt: Write the promotion steps for a prompt change at {company} from merge to 100%, naming the artefact that is built once and reused.

bank.fitNote: every change has an audit trail
bank.practice: {company} uses GitOps: the state of each environment is in a repository, every change is reviewed, and a rollback is a reverted commit with its own record.
bank.failure: A hotfix applied directly in production that the next sync silently undid.
bank.tryIt: List {company}'s infrastructure that should be in code (pools, databases, IAM, secret references, dashboards, alerts), and who reviews changes to each.

travel.practice: {company}'s staging uses the same engine and index type as production with a realistic sample of bookings and fare rules, so tests mean something.
travel.failure: A container that downloads the “latest” model at start-up, so staging and production run different models.
travel.tryIt: Write the differences {company} allows between staging and production (credentials, capacity) and the ones it forbids (images, models, prompts).

harbor.practice: A Harbor candidate improved average accuracy but failed one cross-tenant case; promotion was blocked.
harbor.failure: Treating a green CI badge as proof that every production failure is covered.
harbor.tryIt: In the gated pipeline figure, run each of the four changes and note which gate fails for each. Then write the threshold Harbor uses for cross-tenant leaks.

store.fitNote: cost gates matter at sale volume
store.practice: {company}'s cost gate compares cost per resolved chat with the current release; a cheaper model that resolves fewer chats fails it.
store.failure: Gating on average accuracy only, so a change that broke Hindi answers shipped.
store.tryIt: In the figure, run “model swap to cheaper model” and read which gate fails. Then write {company}'s four gates with one threshold each.

bank.fitNote: critical cases and security gates block release
bank.practice: {company}'s gates block release on any critical-case regression, any cross-customer leak, any critical vulnerability, or a cost rise above the approved limit. Exceptions need a named approver.
bank.failure: Overriding a failed security gate because the release date was fixed.
bank.tryIt: In the figure, run “new tool: send_email” and see which gate fails. Then write {company}'s critical-case list for disputes and the rule for approving an exception.

travel.practice: {company}'s quality gate checks each language separately, so a change that helps English but hurts Tamil is blocked.
travel.failure: One overall quality score that hides a drop in one language.
travel.tryIt: In the figure, run “retrieval k 8 → 20” and read the failing gate. Then write {company}'s per-language quality thresholds.

harbor.practice: Harbor shadows retrieval and generation but never ticket writes; a canary on 3 tenants rolls back automatically if unsupported answers rise.
harbor.failure: Sending shadow traffic to a real write tool.
harbor.tryIt: In the canary figure, start a rollout with a healthy candidate, then with one that regresses at 25%. Then, in the gate-driven figure, untick “rollback rehearsed” and try to advance.

store.practice: {company} shadows new prompts on real chats with order and refund tools stubbed, then canaries to internal staff and a small seller cohort before all shoppers.
store.failure: Shadow traffic reaching the real refund tool, which paid refunds twice.
store.tryIt: In the canary figure, run the regressing candidate and note where it rolls back. Then write {company}'s cohorts (staff, small sellers, all shoppers) and the metric that stops each step.

bank.practice: {company}'s rollout plan includes reconciliation: if a bad version sends wrong letters, rollback stops new ones, and a listed process corrects the ones already sent.
bank.failure: Assuming rollback undoes the customer letters a bad version already sent.
bank.tryIt: In the gate figure, inject a regression at the next stage and advance. Then write the reconciliation steps for letters sent by a bad version.

travel.practice: {company} shadows search and answer generation, but booking changes run only in canary, for a small share of travellers, with automatic rollback if failed bookings rise.
travel.failure: Shadowing the rebooking agent with live supplier holds, which held seats twice.
travel.tryIt: Run the healthy and regressing candidates in the canary figure. Then mark which {company} tools must be stubbed in shadow mode.

harbor.practice: A provider upgrade changed how Harbor's tool calls stream; the parser had to pass compatibility tests before write-capable tasks moved over.
harbor.failure: Assuming the same API method name means the same model behaviour.
harbor.fitNote: streaming tool calls changed with the provider
harbor.tryIt: Read the compatibility report and write the action for each row. Then add a row for “tool-call streaming format” as Harbor found it.

store.practice: A new model wrote 38% longer answers for {company}, which raised cost and made chat slower; length guidance and the cost gate caught it before rollout. (Illustrative.)
store.failure: Calling a “latest” model alias that the provider moved to a new version.
store.tryIt: From the compatibility report, compute the cost change if median output tokens rise 38% and output tokens are 70% of {company}'s per-chat cost.

bank.practice: {company} keeps an inventory of which features use which model versions, with provider retirement dates and owners, and starts compatibility testing three months before each date.
bank.failure: Discovering a model retirement the week it happens.
bank.tryIt: Write {company}'s model inventory table: feature, model version, retirement date, owner, compatibility test status.

travel.practice: When {company} upgrades models, it tests tool-call format for supplier tools, refusal rates and every language separately, and keeps prompt variants per model versioned together.
travel.failure: Reusing prompts tuned for the old model without re-tuning, which raised over-refusal in Hindi.
travel.tryIt: Write {company}'s compatibility checklist for a model upgrade, including a row per language and per supplier tool.

harbor.practice: A recurring Harbor failure on a new document type led to a parser fix and a regression case first; only a remaining extraction gap justified new training data.
harbor.failure: Feeding user corrections straight into training; some are wrong, malicious or out of scope.
harbor.fitNote: fix the parser before adding training data
harbor.tryIt: Step through the improvement loop and write Harbor's retraining triggers. Then say why a parser fix came before new training data.

store.practice: {company}'s support agents edit {assistant}'s drafted replies before sending. The edit fraction per prompt version is a quality metric, and reviewed (draft, sent) pairs become training data.
store.failure: Feeding agents' edits straight into training without review, including edits that added wrong information.
store.tryIt: Write three (draft, sent) reply pairs for chats in chats.json and compute the edit fraction of each (characters changed ÷ length). Then write the review rule before any pair is used for training.

bank.practice: {company}'s staff edit drafted letters before approval. Edits are logged with the trace, and after compliance review they become evaluation cases first and training data only if the gap remains.
bank.failure: Mixing new labels into both evaluation and training sets, so the evaluation measures memory.
bank.tryIt: Write {company}'s retraining triggers (SLO breach, drift, labelled data volume, new base model, policy change) with a threshold for each.

travel.practice: {company} re-runs its full suite every week even without changes, and refreshes the suite each quarter with new messages, including monsoon-season ones.
travel.failure: An evaluation set from last year that never saw this season's disruption questions.
travel.tryIt: Write {company}'s weekly re-evaluation job: suite, thresholds, and what opens a work item.

harbor.practice: Harbor's handover pack names who handles stale ACLs, how to disable a write tool, how to restore an index-and-encoder pair and how to verify recovery.
harbor.failure: Treating a successful demo and an architecture diagram as a handover.
harbor.fitNote: a handover pack with recovery steps
harbor.tryIt: Tick through the operational readiness checklist for Harbor and list the items you could not tick. Then fill one RACI row for index changes.

store.practice: Before each sale, {company} runs an operational readiness review: SLOs, dashboards, runbooks tested, on-call staffed, capacity from measured numbers, budgets set.
store.failure: Treating a successful demo as readiness for sale-day traffic.
store.tryIt: Use the readiness checklist for {assistant}'s sale launch and write the owner for each “must” item.

bank.practice: Every {company} AI system has a named owning team, a system card for governance, and release notes per manifest. Handover to operations includes runbook drills and a period of joint on-call.
bank.failure: A project team handing over an architecture diagram and leaving.
bank.tryIt: Fill the RACI table for {company}'s dispute assistant, then write the handover plan: walkthrough, access, drills, shadow on-call, joint period.

travel.practice: {company}'s rebooking assistant moved from a project team to the operations team with shadow on-call during one disruption season before the project team stepped back.
travel.failure: Handing over in the quiet season and meeting the first disruption without the original team.
travel.tryIt: Write {company}'s release notes for one manifest: what changed, evaluation results, known limits, rollout plan and rollback.

store.scenario: Build a release manifest for {assistant}: code, prompts, order and refund tool schemas, model, embedder and product index. Run the four gates, shadow with refund tools stubbed, inject a regression in the seller canary, and restore the previous manifest.

bank.scenario: Build a release manifest for the dispute assistant with approval records for each gate. Inject a regression in canary, roll back, and write how letters sent by the bad version are found and corrected. Keep the audit trail as evidence.

travel.scenario: Build a release manifest including supplier tool schemas. Gate per language, shadow search only, canary booking changes, inject a regression and restore the previous manifest with a rebooking task as the end-to-end check.

harbor.scenario: Write Harbor's release manifest (code, prompts, tool schemas, model, embedder, index, ACL watermark, eval suite). Run the four gates, shadow without ticket writes, inject a regression in the tenant canary and restore the previous manifest.
